content: Escherichia coli enteritis is a bacterial infection of the gastrointestinal tract caused by pathogenic strains of the Gram-negative rod-shaped bacterium Escherichia coli. It is one of the most common causes of diarrhea globally, accounting for 20% to 50% of all infectious diarrhea cases. In the United States, the incidence is approximately 20 to 30 cases per 100,000 individuals annually. Pathogenic E. coli strains are classified into five main types based on their mechanisms of pathogenicity: Enterotoxigenic E. coli (ETEC), Enteropathogenic E. coli (EPEC), Enterohemorrhagic E. coli (EHEC), Enteroinvasive E. coli (EIEC), and Enteroaggregative E. coli (EAEC). Transmission typically occurs via the fecal-oral route through contaminated food or water. Each strain has a unique pathogenic mechanism. ETEC, EHEC, and EAEC secrete toxins; EIEC invades and migrates within host colonocytes; and EPEC uses an elongation factor (EAF) to cause attachment and effacement of intestinal cells. Risk factors for developing E. coli enteritis include consuming contaminated foods (e.g., undercooked meat, unpasteurized dairy), drinking untreated water, recent travel to developing countries, exposure to infected individuals, daycare or healthcare settings, and recent sexual history involving receptive anal or oral-anal contact. After transmission, the incubation period for pathogenic E. coli strains ranges from 1 to 10 days, during which the patient remains asymptomatic. Early symptoms include diffuse abdominal pain, vomiting, and severe acute watery diarrhea. In some cases, particularly with EHEC and EIEC infections, bloody diarrhea may follow. Most patients recover within 5 to 10 days of symptom onset. However, complications such as hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS), thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP), and acute kidney injury can occur, particularly in EHEC infections. The prognosis for E. coli enteritis is generally excellent, with most cases resolving without long-term sequelae. Identifying the specific causative strain is usually unnecessary for diagnosis and treatment. Diagnostic tests, when performed, may include stool culture, enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), or polymerase chain reaction (PCR). Laboratory findings may show non-specific signs of inflammation or dehydration, such as elevated white blood cell counts, increased inflammatory markers, or metabolic alkalosis. Rehydration is the cornerstone of treatment for E. coli enteritis. Oral rehydration solutions are preferred for patients who can tolerate oral intake, while intravenous rehydration is indicated for those with severe dehydration. Empiric antimicrobial therapy is generally not recommended, as most cases are self-limiting. However, in specific cases of ETEC, EPEC, or EIEC infections, antibiotics such as fluoroquinolones or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) may be considered. Antimicrobial therapy is contraindicated in EHEC infections due to the increased risk of HUS and prolonged bacterial shedding. Antidiarrheal agents are not recommended during the acute phase of infection. Preventive measures include proper hand hygiene with soap and water, safe food handling practices, avoiding consumption of unpasteurized dairy products or juices, and avoiding untreated water. Travelers to high-risk areas should take precautions such as avoiding raw or undercooked foods and drinking only bottled or boiled water. The bacterium Escherichia coli was first cultured by German physician Theodor Escherich in 1885. The first pathogenic strain, Enteropathogenic E. coli (EPEC), was identified in 1945 during outbreaks of infant diarrhea in the United Kingdom. E. coli enteritis must be differentiated from other causes of abdominal pain, diarrhea, and fever, including other infectious agents (bacterial, viral, fungal, or parasitic) and non-infectious conditions such as acute pancreatitis, appendicitis, inflammatory bowel disease, or mesenteric ischemia.
